assertion.prompt: How do zygosity, affected cell lineage and deletion timing influence the relevance of mouse and stem-cell BRPF1 models to variable human heterozygous disease?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Impaired Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cell Maintenance
assertion.rationale: Complete global, early forebrain and hematopoietic loss can cause lethal mouse phenotypes, whereas postnatal CaMKIIa-Cre conditional mice survive and have selective physiological and behavioral effects. Emx1-lineage conditional heterozygotes match human zygosity only within the targeted lineage, not throughout the organism. Human expressivity varies, including a reported individual with normal intellectual development; these observations do not establish normal life expectancy. Human callosal abnormalities are uncommon. Anemia and thrombocytopenia have been reported in a family and in additional individuals in the 2025 cohort, without demonstrating the severe stem-cell failure mechanism of the homozygous hematopoietic mouse model. Global null embryos also have placental and vascular defects with cranial neural tube failure. Zebrafish pharyngeal homeotic transformations establish a developmental role, but have no demonstrated equivalent in human heterozygous craniofacial dysmorphism.

proposed_experiments.name: BRPF1 zygosity-matched allelic series in human iPSC-derived cortical neurons and organoids
proposed_experiments.description: In an isogenic human iPSC background, build a BRPF1 allelic series (heterozygous null, heterozygous patient truncating and missense alleles, homozygous null) and differentiate to cortical neurons and forebrain organoids. Read out H3K23 acetylation and propionylation, chromatin accessibility, intermediate-progenitor (TBR2) abundance, dendritic arborization, and excitatory and inhibitory synaptic physiology. This directly tests whether the heterozygous human state reproduces the null-allele mouse phenotypes and, if so, at what magnitude.

proposed_experiments.name: Test for a BRPF1 DNA methylation episignature in patient blood
proposed_experiments.description: Profile genome-wide DNA methylation in blood from variant-confirmed BRPF1 cases, matched controls and KAT6A/KAT6B cases. A reproducible signature could complement existing patient-cell histone-acylation assays and could be evaluated for variant interpretation. Its diagnostic performance, specificity and sensitivity would require validation; a positive cohort-level result alone would not resolve every variant of uncertain significance.

assertion.prompt: In Wilson disease liver, is the iron-dependent component of injury true ferroptosis, or is it non-specific iron-catalyzed oxidative damage layered onto copper-driven lipid peroxidation?
assertion.rationale: The iron-lowering experiments that motivate this node were performed in LEC rats decades before ferroptosis assays existed, and the human data measure glutathione depletion and thiobarbituric acid reactive substances, which are generic oxidative-stress endpoints rather than ferroptosis markers. Copper is itself a stronger pro-oxidant and thiol-binding agent than iron in liver fractions, so the same readouts are expected from copper alone. Without a ferroptosis-specific rescue and GPX4 or ACSL4 readouts in an ATP7B-deficient system, this entry cannot say whether ferroptosis is a distinct injury pathway here or a relabelling of copper-driven oxidative damage.

assertion.prompt: Mutant TDP-43 knock-in mice develop motor axon degeneration and motor-neuron death with neither nuclear TDP-43 clearance nor TDP-43 aggregates. Does that mean cytoplasmic aggregation and nuclear depletion are also dispensable in human ALS, where both are near-universal findings?
assertion.rationale: TDP-43 Q331K and M337V mice expressed at endogenous levels develop age-dependent, mutant-dependent motor axon degeneration and lower motor neuron death without loss of nuclear TDP-43, without aggregates, and without insoluble TDP-43, while showing both loss and gain of splicing function at selected RNA targets. Taken literally, that dissociates degeneration from the two features this entry treats as the defining lesion of TDP-43 proteinopathy. The mismatch is that the finding is a sufficiency result in an engineered mutant model, whereas ~97% of human ALS — the great majority of it sporadic and not TARDBP-mutant — does show nuclear clearance and phosphorylated cytoplasmic inclusions. The model therefore establishes that an ALS-linked mutant can kill motor neurons through altered splicing alone; it does not establish the temporal position, toxicity, or possible protective role of aggregates in sporadic human disease, and it should not be read as demonstrating that human TDP-43 aggregation is merely a late-stage marker. Resolving this determines whether therapy should target aggregate clearance, TDP-43 localization, or the RNA-processing changes directly.

proposed_experiments.description: In isogenic human iPSC-derived motor neurons, express TDP-43 variants engineered to separate the three features: aggregation-incompetent mutants that retain altered splicing, nuclear-retained mutants, and mutants that aggregate without changing splicing. Compare survival, axonal integrity and cryptic-splicing burden across arms, and benchmark the resulting splicing signatures against nuclear-cleared versus nuclear-preserved motor neurons sampled from sporadic ALS postmortem tissue.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Motor-neuron death in the aggregation-incompetent arm, with a splicing signature matching nuclear-cleared human ALS motor neurons, would extend the mouse result to human cells and argue that RNA misprocessing rather than aggregation is the actionable lesion; survival in that arm together with death in the aggregating arm would confine the mouse finding to mutant-driven disease and keep aggregate species as a human therapeutic target.

assertion.hypothesis_label: Canonical Motor Neuron Proteostatic Failure Model
assertion.description: Progressive upper and lower motor neuron degeneration in ALS is the convergent endpoint of multiple genetic and sporadic insults that ultimately cause proteostatic failure. Key drivers include cytoplasmic mislocalization and aggregation of TDP-43 (in >97% of cases), C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion–derived dipeptide repeats and RNA foci, SOD1 misfolding, FUS/EWSR1 phase-separation defects, impaired autophagy, mitochondrial dysfunction, axonal transport failure, and neuroinflammation. Selective vulnerability of cortical layer-5 Betz cells and spinal alpha motor neurons leads to progressive muscle denervation, weakness, atrophy, and ultimately respiratory failure. Antisense-oligonucleotide therapy targeting SOD1 (tofersen) provides the strongest interventional validation of the SOD1 genetic-pathogenetic axis of this canonical multi-hit model, although that validation rests on target engagement and biomarker lowering rather than on a positive randomized clinical endpoint. The C9orf72 ASO program (BIIB078) was discontinued after a Phase 1 study that showed neither neurofilament reduction nor clinical benefit, indicating that lowering sense-strand repeat RNA alone is insufficient; that single negative program does not by itself establish which of the competing C9orf72 mechanisms — antisense-strand RNA toxicity, dipeptide-repeat proteins, or haploinsufficiency — dominates.
assertion.notes: Retained as CANONICAL. The 2026 openscientist hypothesis-search report (kb/hypotheses/Amyotrophic_Lateral_Sclerosis/canonical_motor_neuron_proteostatic_failure_model) confirms convergent proteostatic failure as the unifying ALS mechanism: TDP-43 proteinopathy in ~97% of cases, SOD1 misfolding, C9orf72 RNA foci and DPRs, FUS phase-separation defects, impaired autophagy, mitochondrial dysfunction, axonal transport failure, and neuroinflammation all converge on motor-neuron degeneration. Tofersen (SOD1 ASO) approval provides the strongest causal validation of the genetic-pathogenetic axes. Four qualifications: (1) the C9orf72-ASO program (BIIB078; Phase 1 discontinued) showed insufficient clinical efficacy — lowering sense-strand repeat RNA does not consistently translate to motor preservation. The 2026 openscientist report reads that failure as evidence that DPR-mediated toxicity dominates; the assessment (assessments/openscientist-assessment-by-codex.yaml, claim c9orf72-failure-mechanism) rejects that inference, since one ASO at one dose range and exposure period cannot separate incomplete target engagement, treatment timing, antisense-strand transcripts, DPR toxicity, haploinsufficiency, or persistent TDP-43 pathology. (2) The "proteostatic failure" framing remains a descriptive convergence rather than a single mechanistic primer — different genetic ALS subtypes follow different upstream paths. (3) Sporadic ALS (~90%) requires environmental/epigenetic modifiers (BMAA, head trauma, aging) that the canonical model does not specify. (4) The tofersen evidence is target-engagement- and biomarker-led: VALOR's prespecified 28-week ALSFRS-R primary endpoint and its clinical secondary endpoints did not separate from placebo, and the longer-term early-start versus delayed-start advantage comes from an open-label extension with substantial attrition, so it is not a blinded randomized efficacy comparison.

value.name: Equine motor neuron disease (vitamin E-deficient horse)
value.genotype: acquired (vitamin E deficiency / chronic oxidative stress)
value.description: Equine motor neuron disease (EMND) is a naturally occurring, acquired lower motor neuron disease of adult horses linked to chronic vitamin E deficiency and oxidative stress, arising in horses stabled without access to pasture. Clinical signs include progressive weight loss, muscle fasciculations, constant weight shifting in the rear limbs, abnormally low head carriage, and excessive recumbency. Pathological findings include type 1 muscle fibre atrophy and lipopigment accumulation in spinal cord capillary endothelium. Unlike classic ALS, which requires combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, EMND involves predominantly lower motor neurons (no upper motor neuron involvement), limiting direct phenotypic equivalence to human ALS.

assertion.name: Tofersen
assertion.description: Antisense oligonucleotide therapy approved for SOD1-ALS that reduces SOD1 protein production, targeting the underlying genetic cause in this subset of patients. The approval rests on target engagement and biomarker lowering rather than on a positive randomized clinical endpoint: over the 28-week randomized period of VALOR tofersen lowered CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light chain but did not improve the prespecified clinical endpoints. A later integrated analysis of VALOR and its open-label extension reported numerically less functional, respiratory, strength and quality-of-life decline over 148 weeks with earlier rather than delayed initiation; because that comparison follows crossover and is open-label with substantial attrition, it is supportive long-term observation rather than a blinded randomized efficacy result.

assertion.prompt: Which cardiac findings reported across m.3243A>G carriers can be assigned specifically to clinically defined MELAS?

assertion.prompt: Why does one variant, m.3243A>G, produce MELAS in some carriers, MIDD or isolated deafness in others, and nothing at all in a further group?
assertion.rationale:
Only about 10% of m.3243A>G carriers in a systematically phenotyped cohort had classical MELAS, while 30% had MIDD, 28% had a combination fitting no recognized syndrome, and 9% were asymptomatic. Heteroplasmy level is the conventional explanation, but measured heteroplasmy explains far less than it is credited with: it did not correlate with disease severity in leukocytes or urinary epithelial cells, and it did not correlate with the grade of retinal dystrophy either. Tissue-specific segregation, nuclear genetic background, mtDNA copy number, and age are all candidate modifiers, and none has been shown to account for the variance. This is what makes genetic counselling and prognosis in m.3243A>G families so weak.
Four public datasets attached here attack the gap from different angles and are worth reading against each other. GSE202747 measures heteroplasmy per cell in a human MELAS tissue and finds it partitions by developmental lineage rather than randomly, which would make any single bulk measurement a poor proxy. GSE56158 varies heteroplasmy experimentally in one nuclear background and finds sharp transcriptional transitions rather than a gradient, offering a mechanism by which a continuous variable yields named syndromes. GSE129091 compares low against high load directly on the MELAS-versus-MIDD axis and reports that the two look alike transcriptionally while differing functionally. GSE85549 moves the question from heteroplasmy to allele, comparing the MELAS m.3243A>G lesion against the myopathy-causing m.3302A>G in the same gene. MSV000088237 extends the allele question outside MT-TL1 entirely, profiling fibroblasts from a patient with the complex I subunit variant m.14453G>A. GSE1462 is the only one that holds genotype constant and varies phenotype in patients - four PEO against four MELAS, all m.3243A>G, all muscle - and its authors read the difference as support for nuclear background as the modifier. That is the right experimental design for this gap, at a sample size and on a 2005 platform that cannot settle it.

assertion.name: STUB1 variants associated with recessive ataxia
assertion.notes: SCAR16 requires two pathogenic STUB1 alleles, homozygous or compound heterozygous. Reported alleles span the tetratricopeptide-repeat, coiled-coil and U-box domains and include missense, nonsense and frameshift changes; the index allele is the U-box missense p.Thr246Met. Heterozygous STUB1 variants cause the allelic dominant disorder SCA48, and some alleles have been reported in both inheritance contexts. Similar biochemical defects alone cannot establish inheritance or predict clinical disease in a heterozygous relative; segregation, age and the specific allele require assessment. A 2019 analysis associated U-box disease alleles with cognitive dysfunction, but it analyzed alleles rather than independent patients and used published cases with some imputed SARA scores. Its ancestry association does not identify a genetic modifier and may be confounded by care or environmental differences. The c.612+11C>G allele below remains a source-classified VUS; its inclusion records the reported uniparental-isodisomy case and does not upgrade it to a proven disease allele.

assertion.name: SOS1 R1131K Transfer-Entropy Signaling Model
assertion.description: Information-theoretic model of bidirectional predictive dependence between SOS1 and RAF from simultaneous single-cell membrane-translocation trajectories. A Gaussian covariance approximation estimates time-resolved transfer entropy in wild-type and Noonan-associated SOS1 R1131K cells with or without MEK inhibition, revealing phase-specific effective regulation consistent with feedback changes or shared hidden inputs.
assertion.base_model: Gaussian-approximation transfer-entropy method of Imaizumi et al. 2022
assertion.model_software: Python 3.9.7, Jupyter, NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn
assertion.model_format: Jupyter Notebook and CSV single-cell time series

modeled_mechanisms.description: Uses SOS1 and RAF membrane-translocation dynamics to measure how R1131K changes effective information flow through the SOS-RAF signaling system. This is an indirect functional readout of the SOS node; RAS-GTP loading is not measured.
modeled_mechanisms.limitations: Transfer entropy quantifies predictive dependence and does not identify a unique biochemical path or prove molecular causality; hidden or common inputs can generate backward information flow. The acute EGF experiment uses SOS1-knockout HeLa cells with ectopic Halo-SOS1 and GFP-RAF, retains endogenous SOS2, pools cells across independent measurements, and does not model development or patient phenotypes. The Gaussian approximation is a first-order treatment of noisy, potentially non-Gaussian trajectories.

readouts.name: Early RAF-to-SOS backward transfer entropy
readouts.interpretation: R1131K increases the early backward information-flow peak, indicating an altered effective feedback regime rather than increased RAS-GTP itself.

readouts.name: Late RAF-to-SOS backward transfer entropy
readouts.interpretation: R1131K decreases the late backward information-flow peak without MEK inhibition, showing that the same allele has opposite phase-specific effects.

readouts.name: Late-phase transfer-entropy abnormality after MEK inhibition
readouts.interpretation: Trametinib removed the late-phase abnormality but did not normalize the early phase, so the rescue is explicitly phase-specific.

variables.description: One-minute single-cell Halo-SOS1 response sequence after EGF stimulation.

variables.name: RAF membrane-translocation trajectory
variables.description: Simultaneously measured single-cell GFP-RAF response sequence.

variables.name: SOS-to-RAF transfer entropy
variables.description: Forward predictive information flow from SOS to RAF.

variables.name: RAF-to-SOS transfer entropy
variables.description: Backward predictive information flow reflecting feedback or shared hidden inputs.

findings.statement: R1131K raises early backward transfer entropy and lowers late backward transfer entropy, revealing a signaling defect not evident from RAF activation or translocation amplitude alone.
Trametinib restores the late-phase transfer-entropy abnormality but not the early-phase abnormality.

assertion.prompt: Is ERK1/2 hyperactivation, rather than ERK5 signaling, the correct driver to assert for RAF1-associated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in Noonan syndrome?
assertion.rationale: The entry's ERK Cascade Hyperactivation node asserts a downstream edge to Cardiomyocyte Hypertrophy on the strength of a mouse RIT1 study showing that MAPK-pathway inhibition alleviates cardiac hypertrophy. A RAF1 S257L/+ iPSC-cardiomyocyte model directly tested the ERK1/2 arm of that pathway and found the opposite: MEK1/2 inhibitors that strongly reduced ERK1/2 phosphorylation had no effect on cell size, while a distinct pathway, ERK5, drove the hypertrophic phenotype. ERK5 is not otherwise modeled anywhere in this entry. The mismatch may reflect a genuine genotype-specific difference (RIT1 vs. RAF1) rather than a wrong edge, but the entry currently cannot distinguish those possibilities because it has no ERK5 node to attach the RAF1 finding to.

assertion.name: DEE114
assertion.description: De novo missense SLC32A1 variants. SLC32A1 encodes the vesicular GABA transporter, which loads GABA into synaptic vesicles, so the lesion is presynaptic and inhibitory. Inherited missense variants in the same gene had already been linked to genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus, and this report establishes that de novo missense variants instead cause a DEE. Two mechanisms were demonstrated in a murine neuronal culture model: three variants lining the putative GABA transport pathway reduced quantal size, consistent with impaired vesicle filling, while an N-terminal variant left quantal size intact but raised presynaptic release probability.

No study has tested the two interventions together, and no human data assign specific clinical features to specific arms; the vosoritide result is consistent with the model but does not rank the arms against each other. assertion.prompt: Is CBP physically depleted from the nucleus into polyglutamine aggregates in Huntington disease, or is it present at normal levels and functionally inhibited by soluble mutant huntingtin? Two bodies of work on the same protein reach opposite answers, and the therapeutic implication differs: clearing aggregates versus disrupting a soluble protein-protein interaction.
assertion.rationale: Both sides are experimentally serious and neither is obviously wrong. The depletion side has cross-system concordance (cell culture, transgenic mice, human postmortem brain) plus a single-cell result in which CBP loss, histone hypo-acetylation and toxicity travel together and are all reversed by CBP overexpression. The no-depletion side tested the model four ways in HD mouse brain, found CBP diffusely nuclear despite abundant inclusions, showed most CBP not co-localized with inclusions by double labelling and electron microscopy, and confirmed by western blot that it was not trapped. The likely reconciliation is that the two are measuring different things: transfected single cells with high mutant huntingtin expression versus whole mouse brain, and functional availability versus total protein. That reconciliation is plausible but untested, which is why this is recorded as a controversy rather than resolved in favour of either. The wider mechanism is not in doubt in the same way. TBP deactivation by soluble oligomers is demonstrated with a chaperone rescue, and the entry's description has been written around functional inhibition accordingly; what remains open is specifically whether CBP is additionally lost from the nucleus.

proposed_experiments.name: CBP abundance against H3K27ac occupancy in graded human HD striatum
proposed_experiments.description: In postmortem HD caudate spanning early and late Vonsattel grades with matched controls, measure total and nuclear CBP protein alongside genome-wide H3K27ac, the mark CBP deposits. Physical depletion and functional inhibition make different predictions that can be told apart in one experiment: depletion predicts reduced CBP protein with globally reduced H3K27ac, whereas functional inhibition predicts preserved CBP protein with H3K27ac lost selectively at mutant-huntingtin-sensitive loci. Running it in human tissue also removes the confound that the existing disagreement may rest on transfected cells versus whole mouse brain.

assertion.prompt: Somatic CAG expansion is the rate-limiting upstream event in HD, and extrasynaptic NMDAR redistribution is the proximate lesion of the excitotoxicity hypothesis, but no experiment has connected them. Does blocking somatic expansion prevent the synaptic-to-extrasynaptic GluN2B shift?
assertion.rationale: The two mechanisms are routinely described as sequential - expansion raises the effective polyQ length, which then disrupts receptor trafficking - but the ordering is asserted rather than demonstrated. Msh3 deletion in Q140 mice abolishes somatic expansion and corrects synaptic and locomotor defects, yet the published readouts do not include compartment-resolved NMDAR localization, so the two mechanisms could equally be parallel consequences of the inherited allele. Which it is decides whether somatic-expansion suppression alone should be expected to normalize excitotoxic vulnerability, or whether the two need separate interventions. The experiment is a straightforward addition to an existing cross rather than new model construction.

assertion.name: Juvenile HD
assertion.subtype_frequency: approximately 1-5% of clinically manifest Huntington disease cases
assertion.description: Juvenile-onset Huntington disease (JHD/JOHD) is defined by motor symptom onset at or before age 20 and accounts for roughly 1-5% of manifest HD. It is driven by the longest CAG expansions - repeat length is usually above 55, around half of cases carry 60 or more repeats, and childhood-onset cases can exceed 80 - which arise by anticipation, most often through paternal transmission (about 80% of cases). The motor phenotype inverts that of adult-onset disease: chorea is uncommon early, while rigidity, axial bradykinesia, dystonia, dysarthria and gait disturbance dominate, and epilepsy, ataxia, spasticity and developmental regression are JHD-specific features. Presentation is frequently non-motor first (behavioural disturbance, declining school performance), which drives misdiagnosis and diagnostic delay. Progression is faster and disease duration shorter than in adult-onset HD. Terminology note: this subtype is historically called the "Westphal variant", but the European Huntington Disease Network JHD working group advises against that usage because the hypokinetic-rigid Westphal phenotype also occurs in adult-onset HD and so is not specific to juvenile onset. The term is retained here only as a synonym, and the preferred label is juvenile-onset HD.

mondo_mappings.mapping_justification: MONDO:0016621 (juvenile Huntington disease) is asserted in MONDO as a direct subclass of MONDO:0007739 (Huntington disease) and is defined by onset of signs and symptoms before 20 years of age, which is exactly the boundary used for this subtype.

assertion.description: Historical but still supported superimposed model proposing that mutant huntingtin and corticostriatal circuit dysfunction enhance NMDA receptor-mediated excitotoxicity in striatal medium spiny neurons. This hypothesis is best viewed as a selective-vulnerability amplifier rather than the sole initiating lesion.
assertion.notes: Retained as ALTERNATIVE. The 2026 openscientist hypothesis-search report (kb/hypotheses/Huntington_Disease/alternative_excitotoxicity) supplies the mechanistic content this framing previously asserted without evidence, and three qualifications a curator should preserve. (1) The proximate lesion is not a global rise in glutamate signalling but a cell-autonomous redistribution of GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors from synaptic to extrasynaptic sites in medium spiny neurons, driven by calpain cleavage of the GluN2B C-terminus and elevated STEP activity and amplified by DAPK1 phosphorylation of GluN2B S1303 - now curated as its own pathophysiology node. (2) The hypothesis is bounded in time. Corticostriatal glutamate release becomes undetectable in HD mice, so excitotoxicity cannot account for neurodegeneration once disconnection has occurred. (3) The human evidence is thin and partly adverse: postmortem in-situ hybridization finds NMDAR subunit mRNA falling with disease severity and reads the astrocytic GLT1 response as compensatory; HD onset-modifier GWAS return mismatch-repair genes and no glutamate-receptor-pathway signal; and NMDA receptor antagonists have failed advanced trials in HD. This human/model gap is recorded as the HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH discussion mismatch_hd_extrasynaptic_nmdar_is_mouse_only. Two of the report's leads were not curated: it cites PMID:11554551 (a 2001 review that says the remacemide HD trial was still ongoing) for trial failure, and asserts a modest memantine benefit in HD that neither cited source reports.

selected_evidence.snippet: At both 6 months and 1 yr, QA lesions showed striking sparing of NADPH-diaphorase neurons as compared with both AMPA and KA lesions, neither of which showed preferential sparing of these neurons.

assertion.hypothesis_label: Double-Strand Break Accumulation as an Expansion-Independent Driver
assertion.description: Genome-wide DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are a driver of HD neuropathology that is mechanistically separable from somatic CAG expansion. On this model the two forms of DNA damage coexist but act through distinct routes: site-specific CAG tract lengthening is driven by active mismatch repair, whereas DSBs arise genome-wide from mutant huntingtin-mediated suppression of non-homologous end joining acting on a background where oxidation converts base excision repair single-strand break intermediates into double-strand breaks. Three observations support separability. (1) DSBs accumulate in zQ175/MSH3(-/-) mice, which cannot somatically expand their allele, alongside the same transcriptional dysfunction seen in expansion-competent zQ175. (2) Pharmacological suppression of DSBs with the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant XJB-5-131 rescues striatal neuron loss and motor performance in HdhQ(150/150) mice while leaving somatic tract length substantially unchanged. (3) Geometry - the CAG tract is under 1e-7 of the genome, so most breaks fall outside it, and Ku70/Ku80 limits end-joining length changes inside it to a few nucleotides, so break burden and tract length are largely decoupled. The therapeutic implication is that expansion suppression and DSB suppression are independent targets that may need to be combined.
assertion.notes: Recorded as EMERGING rather than CANONICAL or ALTERNATIVE. It does not displace the canonical toxic gain-of-function or somatic-expansion models; it adds a parallel arm. Four caveats a curator should preserve. (a) All primary evidence is mouse and, in HdhQ(150/150), male only. (b) The DSBR deficit is measured as delayed clearance of radiation-induced breaks rather than as endogenous repair kinetics. (c) XJB-5-131 suppresses DSB formation upstream via mitochondrial reactive oxygen species; it does not restore end joining, so the rescue shows that break burden matters, not that NHEJ was repaired. (d) No DSBR or NHEJ gene has emerged from human HD GWAS, which the authors attribute to breaks being randomly distributed and NHEJ being reduced rather than absent - this remains an unresolved human/model discrepancy, recorded as the HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH discussion mismatch_hd_dsbr_absent_from_human_gwas.

assertion.prompt: Mitochondrial deficit in HD has two arms, reduced biogenesis through PGC-1alpha repression and reduced clearance through disrupted mitophagy, but their relative contributions to the net deficit have never been measured against each other. Which arm dominates, and does it differ by cell type or disease stage?
assertion.rationale: The two arms have been studied independently and never in the same preparation, so the question has no answer rather than a contested one. It matters because the therapeutic strategies diverge completely: PGC-1alpha activation for a biogenesis-limited deficit, mitophagy induction for a clearance-limited one, and the failure of untargeted bioenergetic supplementation in HD is a reason to want the distinction before designing the next trial. The measurement is tractable - simultaneous turnover reporters in isogenic human neurons - and does not need new model construction.

proposed_experiments.name: Paired mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy flux in isogenic HD striatal neurons
proposed_experiments.description: Use mito-Keima or MitoTimer reporters in HD iPSC-derived striatal neurons and their isogenic CAG-corrected controls to measure mitophagy flux and organelle age distribution in the same cells, alongside mitochondrial mass and PGC-1alpha target expression. Perturb each arm separately - PGC-1alpha overexpression against mitophagy induction - and compare how much of the mitochondrial content and respiratory deficit each recovers.

model_systems.name: Isogenic HD iPSC-derived striatal projection neuron model
model_systems.description: Patient-derived and CAG-corrected striatal neurons carrying live mitochondrial turnover reporters, so production and clearance can be read in the same cell.

perturbations.name: PGC-1alpha restoration
perturbations.description: Overexpression of PGC-1alpha to test the biogenesis arm in isolation.

perturbations.name: Mitophagy induction
perturbations.description: Pharmacological or PINK1/Parkin-driven enhancement of mitophagy to test the clearance arm in isolation.

readouts.name: Mitophagy flux
readouts.description: Rate of delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes, read from the reporter's pH-dependent signal.

readouts.name: Mitochondrial mass and respiratory capacity
readouts.description: Net organelle content and oxygen consumption rate in the same cultures, so each perturbation's rescue can be attributed to its arm.

controls.name: Isogenic CAG-corrected striatal neurons
controls.description: Same genetic background with a nonpathogenic HTT CAG tract.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Whichever single-arm perturbation recovers more of the respiratory deficit identifies the rate-limiting arm. Roughly equal partial rescue with additive combined rescue would mean neither arm is limiting alone and the deficit is genuinely two-sided.
supporting_outcome: A clear asymmetry between the two single-arm rescues, identifying which process limits mitochondrial content in HD striatal neurons.
refuting_outcome: Neither perturbation changes mitochondrial content or respiration, which would place the deficit downstream of both turnover arms.

assertion.description: Mutant huntingtin disrupts transcriptional regulation by interfering with key transcription factors and co-activators (Sp1/TAFII130, CBP, TBP, REST/NRSF), leading to widespread downregulation of neuronal survival genes including BDNF. This is a canonical downstream mechanistic layer in HD, linking mutant huntingtin protein interactions to loss of neuronal maintenance programs. The interference is now understood as functional inhibition by soluble and oligomeric mutant huntingtin - which structurally destabilizes its target - rather than physical trapping of transcription factors inside visible inclusions; the REST/NRSF arm is separate again, and turns on loss of the wild-type protein's cytoplasmic retention of the repressor.
assertion.notes: Retained as CANONICAL, but the mechanism statement was corrected. The 2026 openscientist hypothesis-search report (kb/hypotheses/Huntington_Disease/canonical_transcriptional_dysregulation) surfaced the study that tested the sequestration model directly and did not confirm it: TBP, CBP and Sp1 are diffusely distributed in HD mouse nuclei despite abundant inclusions, and are not trapped in them (PMID:11971872). The resolution is that soluble species do the damage (PMID:15225551), which is also what the entry's own Sp1 evidence says - Sp1 binds soluble, not aggregated, mutant huntingtin. Three further points a curator should keep. (1) The arms are not equally supported: REST/NRSF has genome-wide occupancy data in human postmortem brain plus a loss-of-function phenocopy, Sp1 has human presymptomatic detection plus rescue, and the CBP arm is genuinely contested - recorded as the CONTROVERSY discussion controversy_hd_cbp_depletion_versus_functional_inhibition. (2) Epigenetic silencing runs alongside the transcription-factor arms, and HDAC3 inhibition unexpectedly suppresses striatal CAG expansion as well as correcting gene expression, so the epigenetic layer is not strictly downstream of somatic instability. (3) Therapeutic translation has been poor: no positive phase II or III result for an HDAC inhibitor in HD, and the BET bromodomain inhibitor JQ1 was actively harmful in R6/2 mice while improving wild-type controls. Not integrated from the report: its claim that mitochondrial deficits at postnatal day 0 precede transcriptional change, which rests on a spatial transcriptomics study whose mitochondrial readout is itself transcriptional.

assertion.description: A subset of homozygotes survives to adulthood despite absent detectable SNX14; birth frequency is 9.9% rather than the Mendelian expectation of 25%. Cerebellar RNA from one case demonstrated a 275-base extension of exon 26; Western blot with an antibody targeting sequence upstream of the splice defect detected neither full-length nor shortened SNX14. The allele is strongly supported as causal, but parental genotypes were unavailable. The dogs were euthanized young, limiting assessment of later manifestations.

modeled_mechanisms.description: Spontaneous, early-onset progressive cerebellar ataxia with primary Purkinje-neuron loss and cerebellar atrophy, driven by SNX14 loss of function as in human SCAR20.
modeled_mechanisms.limitations: Two juvenile siblings with a rapid course and early euthanasia. No distinctive facial differences were seen. Hearing appeared normal on examination, but auditory electrophysiology was not performed; cognition was difficult to assess and later manifestations could not be excluded. The model therefore does not establish absence of the human syndromic features.

readouts.interpretation: Primary Purkinje-neuron loss is the structural correlate of the degeneration node in this natural model.

value.name: Impaired Saturated Fatty Acid Processing
value.description: Palmitate-loaded SNX14-knockout U2OS cells accumulate excess free fatty acids without increased fatty-acid uptake. SNX14 co-immunoprecipitates with SCD1 and requires its ER anchor and PXA domain for protection from palmitate. SCD1 overexpression rescues free-fatty-acid accumulation, but direct microsomal assays found no significant reduction of SCD1 enzymatic activity after SNX14 loss. A substrate-presentation or organizational role is proposed; SNX14 is not established as an obligate activator of SCD1.

assertion.description: SCD1-mediated rescue of both free-fatty-acid accumulation and viability supports this connection within engineered U2OS cells.
